claims.text: Under fixed pretax profit P, effective tax rate t and shares N>0, EPS equals P(1-t)/N.
A five-percentage-point tax rate decrease yields a different relative EPS percentage increase.

limitations: This synthetic example does not model financial-reporting adjustments, dilutive securities or legal tax provisions.

sections.formal: Let P denote pretax profit, t the effective tax rate in [0,1], and N the constant number of shares with N>0. Tax expense is tP in this simplified model. After-tax earnings are P−tP=P(1−t), and EPS=P(1−t)/N. Holding P and N fixed, the derivative with respect to t is −P/N, which is negative for positive P.
sections.intuition: The company first earns pretax profit, then pays income taxes; with unchanged pretax profit and unchanged shares, a lower effective tax rate leaves more after-tax earnings for each outstanding share. The amount of the change depends on the tax base and denominator.
misconceptions: Tax rate and earnings per share do not have the same units; one is a ratio and the other a currency amount per share.
sections.title: From pretax profit to earnings per share
sections.visual_description: Side-by-side bars for pretax profit, tax expense and after-tax profit at two effective tax rates, keeping the share count fixed.
sections.worked_example: Given P=100 million, t=0.30 and N=20 million, after-tax profit is 100×(1−0.30)=70 million. Hence EPS=70/20=3.50 per share. If t=0.25, after-tax earnings rise to 75 million and EPS to 75/20=3.75.

sections.formal: For t0=0.30 and t1=0.25, the absolute change in EPS is P(t0−t1)/N. The relative gain is (EPS1−EPS0)/EPS0=(t0−t1)/(1−t0)=0.05/0.70=0.0714286, i.e. approximately 7.14%. This follows only when P and N are constant and the simplified model applies.
sections.intuition: Saying that the tax rate fell by five percentage points is different from saying that earnings per share increased by five percent. The two changes use different starting values as their denominators and therefore have different percentage interpretations.
misconceptions: Five percentage points is not five percent.
A larger EPS number does not necessarily imply higher company value.
sections.title: Percentage points, relative changes and limitations
sections.visual_description: A labeled number line showing the tax rate decrease and a separate EPS bar comparison with relative change annotated.
sections.worked_example: Compare two statements: the tax rate decreases from 30% to 25%, a reduction by 5 percentage points (or 16.67% relative to 30%). EPS rises from 3.50 to 3.75, an increase of 0.25 per share (or 7.14% relative to 3.50). Treating all three numbers as “5%” confuses distinct denominators.
